To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we propose an adaptive transformer architecture which can make predictions after different stages of processing, we investigate different ways of predicting the amount of computation needed for a sequence, and we show that our model can achieve state of the art results while requiring less computational resources.
we can use less computation to achieve the same translation quality, that we can do this without using a large model, and that we can do all this while maintaining a fixed sequence length.

we can train Transformer models which make output predictions at multiple stages, we can use this to predict the amount of computation required for a particular input sequence, and we can use this prediction to adaptively control the number of computations performed by the model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: how much computation is necessary to process a sequence?

the following questions: How can we make sequence to sequence models adapt their computation to the complexity of the input? How do we make the model decide how much computation is enough? How do we train such models?
the problem of efficient training of Transformer models.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the proposed method is an interesting approach to the problem of dynamically adjusting the amount of computation required to process an input sequence, but it does not yet outperform the current state-of-the-art in sequence-to-sequence modeling.
the proposed method, Depth Adaptive Transformer, is a promising and novel approach that can potentially lead to significant improvements in the field of machine translation.
this paper proposes a new way to dynamically adapt the number of layers and the model capacity to the input length of the sequence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can use a Transformer with 4 decoder layers to match the accuracy of a baseline Transformer with 12 layers.
we can achieve a similar accuracy to Transformer but with much less computation, which is especially important for low-resource languages.
we propose a new Transformer architecture that dynamically adapts the depth of the model to the input sequence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to train models with adaptive capacity, and that they are competitive with the best fixed capacity models.
the same model can be used for both fast inference and high accuracy predictions.
it is possible to build Transformer models that are adaptive to different sequence lengths, which can lead to more efficient and accurate models.
